newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks tumble on news of cancer link.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks tumble on news of cancer link.

text.p: Tobacco stocks fell sharply at the opening bell Friday following news that scientists claimed they had established the first direct link on a cellular level between smoking and cancer.
The market sold Philip Morris Cos Inc shares down 3-5/8 in the first hour of trading, to a low of 94-1/2. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp fell one to 26-1/2 and Loews Corp dropped 1-1/8 to 80-1/2.

If accurate, the news might cut consumption levels of cigarettes by convincing the undecided of health risks, but would do little to increase the industry's product liability or compromise its legal defenses in the current onslaught of litigation, analysts said.

"The key point to make is, in 1969 when the (U.S. Surgeon General's) warnings were federally mandated, it shifted the responsibility from the tobacco industry to consumers," said Martin Feldman, tobacco analyst at Smith Barney.
"This discovery does not deteriorate the litigation outlook for the stocks. The current cases are no more threatening to the companies than they were before," Feldman said.

Still unclear was whether the news would dampen sales and whether the industry had lost ground in its battle with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which asserted regulatory control over tobacco products this year.
The industry has sued to block the FDA from regulating tobacco products as drugs, stating that only Congress may confer that regulatory authority.

Oppenheimer & Co analyst Roy Burry echoed Feldman's belief in the industry's legal safety. "If the industry had done this reesearch itself 30 years ago and got this result and hid it, and didn't tell anybody and went out and said cigarettes are fine and advertised them and got people to smoke them, then they would be guilty. But they didnt do that."
Either way, Burry said, "It's not good for business."

Friday's pressure on tobacco stocks came a day after New York City declared it would join the growing number of cities and states suing the industry to recoup public health-care funds spent treating smoking-related illnesses.
"The stocks were driven down because of sentiment, not because of hard, certain fact," Feldman said.

Rodmand & Renshaw analyst Ronald Morrow said the industry would have to deal with the lingering effects of the news on both sales and the FDA fight, but only when the current study -- published Friday in the journal Science -- is confirmed by repeated studies.
"Does it give (the FDA) more ammunition to control the product? Maybe," Morrow said. "But I don't think the public has any illusions about the dangers of cigarette smoking and hasn't for 50 years."
Morrow said Friday's move was an overreaction, adding that he expected Philip Morris shares to end two points lower on the day, following a four- to five-point drop.
